parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: flux linkage and number of turns
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking what flux means for just one single loop of wire in a magnetic field, and what changes if you have many identical loops.
Hint 2: Remember to link the total effect to both the flux through one turn and how many turns the solenoid has, including the unit weber-turns.
parts.proper_answer: Magnetic flux linkage is the product of the magnetic flux through a single turn and the number of turns, $N\Phi = NBA$ for a field normal to the coils.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall What Flux Means For One Turn**
Think of one loop sitting in a magnetic field. The magnetic flux $\Phi$ is $BA$ when the field is normal to the area, a measure of how much field passes through that loop.

Step 2: **Scale Up To Many Turns**
A solenoid has $N$ identical turns linked in series, so the total linkage is $N$ times larger: $$\text{flux linkage} = N\Phi$$ For a uniform field $B$ normal to area $A$, this is $NBA$. That is why it is measured in $\text{Wb turns}$.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which physical law links induced e.m.f. to changing flux linkage, and which part of the $B$-$t$ graph gives the largest rate of change.
Hint 2: Work out the cross-sectional area from the 6.0 cm diameter, converting carefully to metres before using $\pi r^2$.
Hint 3: Read the steepest $\Delta B / \Delta t$ from Fig. 9.2 in tesla per second, then combine it with $N$ and $A$ to get the peak e.m.f.
parts.proper_answer: Area $A = 2.83\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$, steepest $\Delta B/\Delta t \approx 0.23\text{ T s}^{-1}$ on the fall $6.0$ to $7.1\text{ s}$, e.m.f. $= NA\Delta B/\Delta t \approx 0.35\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Faraday's Law**
You are seeing electromagnetic induction. Faraday's law says the magnitude is the rate of change of flux linkage: $$|E| = \left|\frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}\right| = NA\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}$$ because $N$ and $A$ are constant and the field is along the solenoid axis. So you need $A$ and the largest $\Delta B/\Delta t$.

Step 2: **Find The Coil Area**
Diameter $= 6.0\text{ cm} = 0.060\text{ m}$, so radius $r = 0.030\text{ m}$: $$A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.030)^2 \approx 2.83 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$$

Step 3: **Pick The Steepest Slope**
In Fig. 9.2 the rise from $0$ to $250\text{ mT}$ takes about $2.3\text{ s}$, but the fall from $250\text{ mT}$ to zero from $t \approx 6.0\text{ s}$ to $t \approx 7.1\text{ s}$ takes only about $1.1\text{ s}$. That fall is steepest: $$\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} \approx \frac{0.250 - 0}{1.1} \approx 0.23\text{ T s}^{-1}$$

Step 4: **Calculate Maximum e.m.f.**
Now put it together with $N = 540$: $$|E|_{max} = 540 \times 2.83 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.23 \approx 0.35\text{ V}$$ The flat top gives zero e.m.f., and the slower rise gives only about $0.17\text{ V}$, so $0.35\text{ V}$ is the maximum magnitude.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what is happening to the peak height of the dashed $s$-$t$ curve over time and recall the general name for loss of amplitude.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Name The Loss Of Amplitude**
The dashed curve keeps oscillating with the same period but its amplitude steadily shrinks. That gradual loss of oscillatory energy and amplitude is called damping.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: effect of slits on current paths
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to magnetic flux through the copper as it swings in and out of the magnet gap.
Hint 2: Consider what Faraday's law says must appear in a conductor when that flux changes, and in which direction the effect acts by Lenz's law.
Hint 3: Compare how easily those induced currents can flow in a solid sheet X versus the slotted sheet Y shown in Fig. 9.4.
Hint 4: Link the size of those currents to the amount of braking and decide which sheet matches the strongly decaying dashed curve in Fig. 9.5.
parts.proper_answer: Dashed line is sheet X. Moving sheet cuts field, changing flux induces e.m.f. and eddy currents whose direction opposes the motion, dissipating energy. Slits in Y restrict eddy currents so Y is less damped, solid curve. Hence X shows greater damping, dashed curve.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Changing Flux Induces An e.m.f.**
As the pendulum swings, the copper moves through the magnet gap so the amount of field it cuts keeps changing. That means the magnetic flux through the metal changes, so by Faraday's law an e.m.f. is induced in the copper.

Step 2: **Eddy Currents Oppose The Motion**
Because copper is a conductor, that e.m.f. drives circulating eddy currents. By Lenz's law their magnetic effect opposes the change that caused them, so they produce a braking force on the swing. The electrical energy is dissipated as heat in the resistance of the copper, removing mechanical energy.

Step 3: **Why X Damps More Than Y**
Sheet X is solid, so large uninterrupted loops can flow and the braking is strong. Sheet Y is cut into thin strips, which breaks up the current paths. The induced currents in Y are much smaller, so the braking force and energy loss are much smaller.

Step 4: **Match To The Graph**
Fig. 9.5 shows the dashed line decaying quickly to almost zero while the solid line keeps almost constant amplitude. The quickly decaying motion must be the strongly damped one, so the dashed line is sheet X and the solid line is sheet Y.
